OSPBEIJ 20: This course is a survey of China's economic trajectory since the 1980s. Students should finish the course with an understanding of the following issues: In what ways is China's rise historically unprecedented, and in what ways not; What explains China's remarkably rapid China's economic rise; How do China's political institutions guide its economy; How does the structure of China's economy differ from virtually all others; What current challenges will shape China's future? NOTE: OSPBEIJ 20 is the same as -Sociology 175/275/Global 194-. Students may not earn credit for both.
OSPBEIJ 25: This is a research seminar on the establishment of industrial parks by Chinese local governments and firms in Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) countries, with a focus on Southeast Asia. The goal is to provide an in-depth understanding of how local governments are being proactive, using international investment to complement their domestic development strategies, and taking advantage of the BRI, a key initiative of China's efforts to globalize. The course will begin with key readings on the BRI, followed by students doing in depth case studies of local Chinese investments abroad to see how the BRI has played out in different countries and different sectors over time. nn
OSPBEIJ 30: This course is a survey course of economic development in China with emphasis on understanding the process of economic reform, transition, and development during the past 20 years. China now has one of the fastest growing economies in the world, and China and the Chinese economy now receive a great deal of attention in the mass media. One goal of the course is to help students develop an informed perspective on the different historical stages, economic and political rationale, and effectiveness of the economic policies and institutional changes that have shaped China's economic emergence. In this sense, the course is very much a selected topics course with a broad range of topics covered, ranging from China's historical legacies, the Mao era, and the policies that generated growth in the post-Mao period. NOTE: Same as ECON 131. Students may not earn credit for both OSPBEIJ 30 and ECON 131.
OSPBEIJ 35: This course is intended to provide background information on China and its foreign policies and relevant strategies. The first part of the course covers the PRC's thinking about strategy, its territorial disputes with its neighbors, history of use of force in the region and how it makes foreign and security policy. The second part will focus on learning about the history and nature of Chinese foreign policy, with a particular emphasis on contemporary China. We will look at the state of research on contemporary China foreign policy to include Chinese economic policy, role in international institutions, and trends in relations with Northeast Asia, the United States, and the world. Note: 4 sessions (4/30, 5/2, 5/7 and 5/9) 3 hours each.
OSPBEIJ 40: The end of the Cold War in 1991 was a glorious moment to be a multilateralist and liberal democrat. Even previously closed-off China had chosen the path of economic liberalization and some political reform. It seemed like the whole world wanted to become a democracy and join the democratic community of states. Today, great power competition is back with many describing our present era as a "New Cold War" between the United States and China. How did the international system go from euphoria about democracy, globalization, the West, and the United States three decades ago, to uncertainty about democracy, doubt about the liberal international order, and fear about the rise of illiberal great powers? Moreover, is the Cold War label an illuminating or distorting analogy, and how stable or enduring is this current moment of global confrontation? This course seeks to analyze contemporary U.S.-China relations. We will begin by reviewing the major theories in IR, from both Western and Chinese scholars. Then, in our second session, we will study the historical origins of U.S.-China relations, examining the interplay between three central drivers of international relations ? power, regime types, and leaders ? over time. The third part of the course will focus on assessing the similarities and differences between the Cold War and U.S.-China relations today along three dimensions of the international system: (1) power, (2) ideology, and (3) competing conceptions of global order. The fourth and final part of the course will discuss a set of concrete policy recommendations for how U.S. leaders can (and should) meet the challenge of great power competition in the 21st century. The main text for this course will be the draft of Professor McFaul's upcoming book, tentatively called Great Power Competition in the 21st Century: Lessons from the Cold War for Competing with China and Russia Today, as well as accompanying academic books and articles. Sessions: 4/1, 4/3, 4/8, 4/10
OSPBEIJ 45: Contemporary China presents many puzzles for the social sciences: Recurring cycles of centralization and decentralization, a strong state coexists with considerable variations across localities, the prevalence of informal institutions in Chinese bureaucracy, and high mobilizational capacities accompanied with bureaucratic inertia. The goal of this course is to examine stable patterns of behaviors - individual and organizational - and the underlying logics of governance in contemporary China. Drawing on a rich literature of direct observation and empirical research in the post-Mao era, this course discusses a set of analytical concepts and theoretical models and apply them to interpret a wide range of social and organizational phenomena in China, and to consider their implications for the future of China. NOTE: Same as INTLPOL 224C, SOC 216, SOC 116. Students may not earn credit for both OSPBEIJ 45 and INTLPOL 224C, SOC 216, SOC 116.
OSPBEIJ 50: Technology is one of the most powerful forces in our political and social world. In this course we attempt to understand how technology is shaping governance and society in China. By engaging with diverse sources from social science research to on-the-ground practitioners, we will try to understand the role that technology has and continues to play in China's current governance and situate China's approach in a comparative, global context. We will explore a range of technological innovations, with a focus on digital communication technologies and applications of machine learning and generative AI.
OSPBEIJ 55: This five-unit seminar will be a geographically focused introduction to a domain of scholarly inquiry. The intersection of health, culture, and politics has been a fount for significant study over recent decades. An especially generative region for this form of inquiry has been Asia and more particularly China. In this course, students will pursue two main learning goals: (1) acquiring the competency to evaluate new scholarly research conducted by anthropologists on topics pertaining to health and politics in Chinese cultural contexts and (2) gaining hands-on experience conducting ethnographic inquiry on allied topics. Class will meet twice a week and will promote learning goals in a two-step choreography. Part one of each session will entail two students (a) presenting prepared reflections on that day's assigned reading, (b) raising pertinent questions about the text, and (c) guiding discussion (with help from the instructor). These presentations will prime every student not only to delve deeply into our readings but also hone their presentation and leadership skills. Prof. Kohrman will fill out class meetings with brief lectures where necessary. The second half of each class session will be devoted to skill acquisition fundamental to conducting ethnographic research. These will include designing research questions, choosing and deploying qualitative methods, writing field notes, analyzing and presenting findings, and grappling with ethics of academic inquiry. Note: Same as ANTHRO 248, ANTHRO 148, CHINA 155A, CHINA 255A. Students may not earn credit for both OSPBEIJ 55 and ANTHRO 248, ANTHRO 148, CHINA 155A, CHINA 255A.
OSPBEIJ 60: This course introduces to students the cognitive norms of modern Chinese, as well as its developmental history in greater China. Students will learn how Chinese has been made modern as ways of social progressions in relation to a host of cultural-political events and popular thoughts over the past century in various Chinese speech communities. Language planning for a standard pronunciation, grammar, orthography, etc. for China, a linguistically most diverse country where people commonly grow up speaking mutually unintelligible languages, unfolded over a course of socio-political conflicts in the contexts of "progressive," "patriotic," or "scientific" transformations of a country of abject poverty into a major world power again. Special attention will be given to the socio-linguistic changes following language contacts between Chinese and English/Japanese languages. Cultural and societal perspectives and biases in trendy internet neologisms and perpetuated by large language models will be critically analyzed in search of the socio-cultural origins of these human behaviors. Although a student with some knowledge of a modern Chinese language will easily gain much more depth from the course, prior Chinese knowledge is not required.
OSPBEIJ 70: As two of the most-consequential global powers, the United States and China have great influence on many complex transnational challenges, including nuclear proliferation, health security, economic development, cyberspace, and energy development. None of these challenges can be managed by the United States or China alone; none can be managed successfully without some level of U.S.-China coordination. U.S. and Chinese approaches to global issues often differ, making cooperation difficult. This unique course features lecturers from both Stanford University and Peking University, and students from both schools attend. The course will examine American and Chinese perceptions of and approaches to resolving a number of different transnational challenges with the goal of identifying obstacles to and opportunities for cooperation in light of evolving policies and circumstances in both countries.
OSPBEIJ 80: Corporations are the core of modern economies, and China's leading corporations are both new and structured in ways that contrast in striking ways with those elsewhere in the world. Analyzing the history of China's leading corporations is a superb way of understanding the transformation of the country's economy over the past 30 years and the inner workings of the Chinese model of development. This seminar will focus on the formation, development, and global expansion of business activities by large Chinese corporations, something that has accelerated over the past two decades. Each student will complete a detailed case history of a major Chinese corporation. Students will make two classroom presentations of their final case histories and submit a final research paper. Enrollment is limited to 12.
OSPBEIJ 90: This course examines China's energy transition over the past two decades and the country's emergence as a global leader in clean energy manufacturing and adoption. Combining lectures, discussions, case studies, and field visits to firms and energy sites, the course explores why China has pursued this transition and how its electricity, solar, wind, battery, and electric vehicle sectors have developed. Students will study the roles of industrial policy, environmental regulation, market competition, infrastructure investment, supply chains, engineering talent, and manufacturing know-how in shaping China's clean energy industries. The course also considers the global implications of China's rise in clean energy, including the effects of low-cost Chinese technologies on global decarbonization, trade tensions and industrial policy responses, Chinese outbound investment, and lessons for other countries seeking to build green industries while decarbonizing at scale.
